div.div: is fundamentally different from CPU or Memory because, in a standard Kubernetes setup, it is an Unmanaged Resource

div.div: K8s treats the network like an "all-you-can-eat" buffet, which can lead to significant stability issues.

div.div: By default, Kubernetes has no built-in concept of network-requests or network-limits in the Pod spec.

div.div: The Problem: If you have a high-traffic API pod and a backup-sync pod on the same node, the backup pod could suddenly start a 10Gbps transfer.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 498px; height: 1px; padding-top: 360px; margin-left: 1021px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: The Result: It will saturate the node's physical Network Interface Card (NIC). Your API pod's latency will spike, or it might start dropping connections entirely, even though its CPU and Memory usage look perfectly normal.

div.div: Shared Fate: Every pod on that node shares the same "pipe" to the outside world.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.div: Silent Failures: Most monitoring tools focus on Pod-level metrics. You might see your application failing but not realize it's because a completely unrelated Pod in a different namespace is hogging the node's bandwidth.

div.div: certain instance types (like the m5n or c5n variants) have dedicated "Network Cards" for EBS and standard traffic. This prevents your database's disk I/O (EBS) from fighting with your user traffic for the same bandwidth!
